notes.meaning: The church in Antioch had several gifted leaders who were prophets and teachers. These men came from very different backgrounds and social ranks, showing how the gospel brings diverse people together into one family. Manaen had even grown up in the royal court with Herod Antipas, yet chose to leave high society behind to serve the flock of Christ.

While these leaders were worshiping the Lord and fasting to seek His guidance, the Holy Spirit gave them direct instructions. The Spirit told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for a special missionary assignment to which He had called them. This makes it clear that the Holy Spirit is a divine Person who actively directs the work of the church.

The church leaders spent more time in prayer and fasting before placing their hands on Barnabas and Saul to send them out. Laying on hands was a public sign of blessing, recommending the two men to God's care and power for this hard task. The congregation willingly gave up two of its finest teachers for the sake of taking the good news to new lands.

Barnabas and Saul went down to the seaport of Seleucia and sailed across the sea to the island of Cyprus. Luke emphasizes that the Holy Spirit was the true authority sending them on their way. Cyprus was a natural first stop because it was close by, and it was also the homeland of Barnabas.

After arriving at the port of Salamis, they began proclaiming the message of God in the Jewish synagogues. Going to the Jews first followed the pattern of offering salvation to God's covenant people before reaching out to others. John Mark traveled alongside them to help with practical duties and daily needs so the apostles could focus on preaching.

The missionaries traveled through the entire island until they arrived at the capital city of Paphos on the western shore. There they encountered a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus, who claimed to have supernatural powers. Paphos was known for its famous temple to Venus, making it a place marked by deep spiritual deception and moral darkness.

The sorcerer had attached himself to Sergius Paulus, the Roman proconsul who governed the island. Even though he held high political power, the governor was an intelligent and thoughtful man who invited Barnabas and Saul to speak because he wanted to hear God's word. Wise leaders show true good sense when they seek out God's truth for themselves.

The sorcerer, who also went by the title Elymas, strongly opposed the missionaries and tried to keep the governor from believing. He knew that if the governor accepted the gospel, his own influence and deceitful trade would be finished. Satan often works hard to hinder influential people from faith because their choices affect so many others.

Saul, who is here called Paul for the first time in Acts, was filled with a fresh surge of power from the Holy Spirit. He looked straight into the eyes of Elymas with holy courage to confront his evil deeds. From this point on, Luke calls him by his Roman name, Paul, as his great mission among the Gentiles begins.

Paul openly rebuked the sorcerer as a deceitful trickster and an enemy of everything that is good and right. Although the man went by the name Bar-Jesus, which means son of a savior, Paul declared that his actions proved him to be a true child of the devil. The magician was actively twisting God's straight path of truth to keep others from finding life.

Paul announced God's judgment against Elymas, telling him that he would be struck blind for a time. Immediately a thick mist and total darkness covered his eyes, leaving him to grope around and beg someone to lead him by the hand. His physical blindness was a fitting sign of the spiritual darkness he had been trying to spread.

When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed the message of the gospel. He was astonished not only by the miracle itself, but by the power and truth of the teaching about the Lord. God used this direct victory over evil to bring an important Roman ruler into genuine faith.

Paul and his group sailed northwest from Paphos across the sea to Perga in the region of Pamphylia. At this stop, John Mark decided to leave them and return home to Jerusalem. Paul viewed this departure as an unfaithful desertion, likely caused by fear of the rough mountain journey ahead or shrinking from hardship.

Traveling inland from Perga through dangerous mountain passes, Paul and Barnabas arrived at Pisidian Antioch. On the Sabbath, they entered the local synagogue and sat down among the worshipers. Even while on a mission to the Gentiles, they continued their practice of bringing the good news to the Jews first.

After the regular Sabbath readings from the Law of Moses and the Prophets, the synagogue leaders sent an invitation to the visitors. They politely asked Paul and Barnabas if they had any word of encouragement or teaching to share with the congregation. This open invitation gave Paul the exact opportunity he needed to preach Christ from the Scriptures.

Paul stood up, signaled with his hand to quiet the room, and began to speak. He addressed both the native Israelites and the Gentile God-fearers who worshiped with them in the synagogue. This began Paul's first recorded sermon in Acts, where he traced the whole story of God's promises to His people.

Paul began his message by reminding his hearers that God chose the fathers of Israel purely out of His own grace. While they were living as oppressed strangers in Egypt, God built them into a great nation and brought them out with His mighty power. Israel's greatness did not come from their own merit, but from God's faithful love.

God patiently looked after the people of Israel during forty years of wandering in the desert. Even though they grumbled, doubted, and tested His patience, He mercifully fed them and carried them through the wilderness. His loving care remained steady despite their repeated rebellion.

God wiped out seven wicked nations living in Canaan so He could give their land to Israel as a permanent home. The conquest was achieved by God's sovereign power, not by Israel's own military strength. This fulfilled the ancient promise He had sworn to the patriarchs centuries before.

After dividing the land, God gave them leaders called judges for about 450 years, lasting until the time of Samuel the prophet. Whenever the nation fell into trouble because of sin, God answered their cries and sent judges to rescue them from their enemies. This long period highlighted God's tireless mercy during centuries of human failure.

When the people demanded an earthly king like the nations around them, God gave them Saul, son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, who ruled forty years. This king belonged to the very same tribe as the apostle Paul himself. Yet Saul's troubled reign proved that human kings cannot cure the rebellious hearts of the people.

After removing Saul because of his disobedience, God raised up David to be their king. God declared that David was a man after His own heart who would carry out His will. While David was far from sinless, his public life was marked by genuine love for God, obedience to His law, and deep repentance.

Paul brought his historical survey directly to its main point: God brought to Israel the Savior Jesus from the family line of David, exactly as promised. The name Jesus means Savior, and His coming fulfilled centuries of Old Testament prophecy. All of Israel's past history was moving toward the arrival of this one true King.

Before Jesus began His public ministry, John the Baptist prepared the way by preaching a baptism of repentance to all Israel. John called people to turn away from their sins and seek God so they would be ready to welcome their Messiah. This proved that Jesus' arrival was no sudden surprise, but was announced beforehand by a recognized prophet.

As John was finishing his race and ministry, he made it clear to everyone that he was not the promised Messiah. Instead, he pointed to Jesus, saying he was not even worthy to perform the humble servant duty of untying His sandals. John showed that all earlier messengers exist only to point people to Christ.

Paul warmly addressed his listeners, including both the physical descendants of Abraham and the Gentile God-fearers sitting with them. He announced that this message of rescue from sin had been sent straight to them. God was offering His great salvation to the Jewish community first, urging every person present to welcome the Savior.
